## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cakkavākajātaka* (Ja 451) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1887]. In the frame story (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha relates the discourse at Jetavana regarding a greedy monk (*lolabhikkhu*) who neglected his monastic duties to constantly inquire after food invitations and meat [Fausböll 1887]. To show that this monk's excessive craving had caused him hardship in the past, the Buddha recounts the story of the past (*atītavatthu*).

In the past, the Bodhisatta was born as a ruddy goose or red-duck (*cakkavāka*) dwelling with his mate along the Ganges [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1887]. A greedy crow, noticing the duck's radiant and well-conditioned form, inquires with the opening verse beginning *Vaṇṇavā abhirūpo si* ("Fine-coloured art thou"), assuming the duck achieves beauty by gorging on river fish [Fausböll 1887]. The Bodhisatta explains that his beauty and happiness do not arise from slaughter or meat, but from harmlessness, virtue, and contented living [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1887]. In the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the crow is identified with the greedy monk, the female duck with Rāhula's mother, and the ruddy duck with the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1887].
